Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2
growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of
GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab
dilution. We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs
likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity
J.P. Morgan Securities (Asia Pacific) Limited/ J.P.
and cost-down measures. Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand
pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain
tight into 2026. While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in
revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less
intense than feared. As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with
low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy
growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength
in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates
by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of
NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market
is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity
emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and
GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.
Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better:  TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin
guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600
bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion
since 1Q25. Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures
have also contributed to keeping costs under check. But for the steep TWD
appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by
now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence. We
believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower
utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues). But 4Q25 should be the near-
term bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from
early 2026. We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026,
despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.
Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3
migration kicking in:  TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth
appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from
sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from
China, after H20 resumption, in our view. We expect Datacenter AI growth
expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by
strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to
migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution
from HBM base-dies. We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely
to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA
starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

now the norm:  As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of
growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm. Hence, 5-6% wafer
shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive
capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term. For 2026,
we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects
increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices. We
believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of
CoWoS. Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with
upside risk from Intel:  We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026,
a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year
revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing
yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears
increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship
SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer
demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all
leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a
much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk
- we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks
increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k
wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's
client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q:  Investor attention
is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.  We believe that TSMC
is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not
factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point. TSMC also appears to be
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in
our view). We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp
slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been
better than feared. Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less
price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for
many years. We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc.
in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3
capacity since 2H24. Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in
better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend
growth ahead:  TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate
continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand. We expect 2026
capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and
continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2 nd  AZ Fab
and construction of 3 rd  and 4 th  AZ Fab in 2026). We also expect N2 demand to be upsized
in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing. We
believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation,
and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

We anticipate that AI growth expectations are likely to be revised up in the following
quarters due to sustained AI demand and potential upside from China (driven by lifting
of H20 restrictions). In addition, management believes that the supply-demand gap for
CoWoS will persist into 2026, exceeding investors' expectations of a balanced CoWoS
As Apple and other flagship smartphone manufacturers transition from N3 to N2 in
2026, we expect many AI accelerators to shift to the N3P and N3X processes starting in
late 2025, with additional contributions from HBM base-die revenues once HBM4
adoption increases in 2H26. We project N3 utilization to remain above 100% in 2026,
with ASP for N3 increasing by 19% YoY (price hike and better mix due to higher HPC
share), contributing to a 35% YoY revenue growth for N3 in 2026. Overall, we
anticipate 50-60% growth in datacenter AI revenue in 2026.

Pricing uptick coming through; Double-digit blended ASP
TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases,
including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25. Given strong pricing power and intention to raise
pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid
teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward. As a
result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth,
which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over
With TSMC indicating that capacity remains tight, particularly for N5 and N3, and a
faster ramp-up of N2, we anticipate pricing to rise in 2026 (6-10% increase in leading-
edge wafer prices, along with higher pricing for overseas fabs) to offset cost increases,
some impact of TWD appreciation and overseas expansion.

In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth
in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s. While we’ve already highlighted the
potential guidance raise ( link ), the magnitude turns out to be slightly above our
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around
10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of
1%/6% qoq decline. We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in
3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on
tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for
TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that
tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared. While we do believe that there has
been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40%
yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to
eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no
significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more
guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy)
in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong
N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of
capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and
4th AZ Fab in 2026). In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs
a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
While the Capex seems to be high in terms of dollar amount, management also
emphasized that sales growth would outgrow the capex growth. We anticipate capital
intensity likely to be down to ~30% in 2027 versus 40-50% in 2023-25.

We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly
position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and
N2) and industry-leading packaging technology. We believe TSMC could grow low-mid
30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pick-
up (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026. Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3
yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the
positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the
impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in
2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

records.text: The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
records.raw_text:
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of 
GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab 
dilution. We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs 
likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity 
and cost-down measures. Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand 
pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain 
tight into 2026. While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in 
revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less 
intense than feared. As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with 
low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy 
growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength 
in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates 
by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of 
NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market 
is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity 
emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and 
GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy 
growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength 
in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates 
by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of 
NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market 
is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity 
emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and 
GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

records.text: • Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
records.raw_text:
• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin 
guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 
bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion 
since 1Q25. Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures 
have also contributed to keeping costs under check. But for the steep TWD 
appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by 
now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence. We 
believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower 
utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues). But 4Q25 should be the near-
term bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from 
early 2026. We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, 
despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

records.text: • Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
records.raw_text:
• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 
migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth 
appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from 
sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from 
China, after H20 resumption, in our view. We expect Datacenter AI growth 
expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029). 
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by 
strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to 
migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution 
from HBM base-dies. We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely 
to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA 
starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

records.text: now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
records.raw_text:
now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of 
growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm. Hence, 5-6% wafer 
shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive 
capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term. For 2026, 
we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects 
increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices. We 
believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of 
CoWoS. Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.

records.text: • N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
records.raw_text:
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with 
upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, 
a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year 
revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing 
yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears 
increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship 
SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer 
demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all 
leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a 
much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk 
- we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks 
increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k 
wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's 
client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.

records.text: • Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
records.raw_text:
• Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention 
is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.  We believe that TSMC 
is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not 
factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point. TSMC also appears to be 
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in 
our view). We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp 
slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been 
better than feared. Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less 
price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for 
many years. We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. 
in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 
capacity since 2H24. Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in 
better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.

records.text: • Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
records.raw_text:
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend 
growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate 
continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand. We expect 2026 
capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and 
continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab 
and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026). We also expect N2 demand to be upsized 
in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing. We 
believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, 
and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).  Even in this

underlying pricing power and operational efficiency. Without the recent TWD 
appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this 
point.

records.text: TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases, including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25.
records.raw_text:
TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases, 
including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25. Given strong pricing power and intention to raise 
pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid 
teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward. As a 
result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth, 
which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over 
the long term.

Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around 
10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of

records.text: TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
records.raw_text:
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy). 
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no 
significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more 
guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.

records.raw_text:
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy). 
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no 
significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more 
guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
records.repair_method: same-zone reflow, heading/bullet/gap boundaries, decimal-safe sentence split

records.text: However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy) in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
records.raw_text:
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy) 
in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong 
N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of 
capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 
4th AZ Fab in 2026). In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs 
a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.

source_excerpt.text: The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
source_excerpt.raw_text:
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of 
GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab 
dilution. We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs 
likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity 
and cost-down measures. Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand 
pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain 
tight into 2026. While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in 
revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less 
intense than feared. As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with 
low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy 
growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength 
in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates 
by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of 
NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market 
is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity 
emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and 
GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

Investment Thesis

due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge
AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and
industry-leading packaging technology. We believe TSMC
could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy
growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pick-up (e.g.
CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity
remaining tight into 2026. Additionally, we anticipate the GM to
rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and
accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.

now the norm:  As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of
growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm. Hence, 5-6% wafer
shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive
capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term. For 2026,
we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects
increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices. We
believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of
CoWoS. Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
•
N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with
upside risk from Intel:  We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026,
a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year
revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing
yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears
increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship
SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer
demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all
leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a
much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk
- we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks
increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k
wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's
client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
•
Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q:  Investor attention
is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.  We believe that TSMC
is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not
factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point. TSMC also appears to be
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in
our view). We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp
slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been
better than feared. Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less
price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for
many years. We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc.
in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3
capacity since 2H24. Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in
better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
•
Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend
growth ahead:  TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate
continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand. We expect 2026
capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and
continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2 nd  AZ Fab
and construction of 3 rd  and 4 th  AZ Fab in 2026). We also expect N2 demand to be upsized
in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing. We
believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation,
and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.
3

Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better
TSMC reported a stronger-than-expected 2Q GM of 58.6%, beating both JPMe and
Consensus by 0.7-1ppt and reaching the high-end of its guidance (57-59%) despite
unfavorable FX (around 125bps impact) thanks to higher-than-expected UTR and cost
improvement efforts.
Company guided 3Q rev to grow 8% qoq at mid point, with GM likely at 55.5-57.5%
(down 2.1ppts qoq at mid point). The margin guidance is quite impressive in our view,
considering a 600 bps drag from TWD and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since
1Q25.
While 4Q GM would likely further decline with the UTR draw down, we expect 4Q25
to be the near-term bottom for GMs.
2H25 should be the period with maximum stress on GMs (fastest period of TWD
appreciation so far in 3Q25, overseas cost dilution, some negate demand impact
dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).  Even in this
period, TSMC appears to be able to hold GMs well above 53%, demonstrating its
underlying pricing power and operational efficiency. Without the recent TWD
appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this
point.
With price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026, we expect GMs to
remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2
starts ramping up.

We anticipate that AI growth expectations are likely to be revised up in the following
quarters due to sustained AI demand and potential upside from China (driven by lifting
of H20 restrictions). In addition, management believes that the supply-demand gap for
CoWoS will persist into 2026, exceeding investors' expectations of a balanced CoWoS
demand by that year.
As Apple and other flagship smartphone manufacturers transition from N3 to N2 in
2026, we expect many AI accelerators to shift to the N3P and N3X processes starting in
late 2025, with additional contributions from HBM base-die revenues once HBM4
adoption increases in 2H26. We project N3 utilization to remain above 100% in 2026,
with ASP for N3 increasing by 19% YoY (price hike and better mix due to higher HPC
share), contributing to a 35% YoY revenue growth for N3 in 2026. Overall, we
anticipate 50-60% growth in datacenter AI revenue in 2026.

Pricing uptick coming through; Double-digit blended ASP
increases now the norm
TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases,
including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25. Given strong pricing power and intention to raise
pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid
teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward. As a
result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth,
which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over
the long term.
With TSMC indicating that capacity remains tight, particularly for N5 and N3, and a
faster ramp-up of N2, we anticipate pricing to rise in 2026 (6-10% increase in leading-
edge wafer prices, along with higher pricing for overseas fabs) to offset cost increases,
some impact of TWD appreciation and overseas expansion.
5

Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness
in 4Q
In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth
in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s. While we’ve already highlighted the
potential guidance raise ( link ), the magnitude turns out to be slightly above our
expectation of high-20s.
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around
10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of
1%/6% qoq decline. We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in
3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on
tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for
TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in
our view).
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that
tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared. While we do believe that there has
been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40%
yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and
N3 capacity since 2H24.
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to
eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

expectation of high-20s.
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around
10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of
1%/6% qoq decline. We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in
3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on
tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for
TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be
anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in
our view).
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that
tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared. While we do believe that there has
been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40%
yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and
N3 capacity since 2H24.
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to
eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

Capex outlook and Dividend growth
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no
significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more
guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy)
in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong
N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of
capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and
4th AZ Fab in 2026). In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs
a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
While the Capex seems to be high in terms of dollar amount, management also
emphasized that sales growth would outgrow the capex growth. We anticipate capital
intensity likely to be down to ~30% in 2027 versus 40-50% in 2023-25.
Meanwhile, we believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong
FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends
reaching NT$33 levels.

improvement efforts

•
N3: 24% of sales
•
N5: 36% of sales
•
N7: 14% of sales
Revenue mix by platform
•
HPC up 14% QoQ (60% of sales)
•
Smartphones up 7% QoQ (27% of sales)
3Q25 outlook
•
Revenue US$31.8-33.0bn, up 8% QoQ at midpoint
•
3Q25 will be driven by leading edge process
•
GM 55.5-57.5%, due to continued unfavored FX (NT$32.88 in 1Q25 vs. NT$31.05
in 2Q25) and more pronounced dilution from overseas fabs in Kumamoto and
Arizona
•
FX NT$29
•
OPM 45.5-47.5%
•
Maintain 2025 capex to be US$38-42bn
Overseas dilution
•
Overseas dilution to continue in the next five years, starting from 2025
•
GM dilution from overseas to begin with 2-3ppts in early stage and 3-4ppts in later
stage
•
TSMC will leverage increasing size in AZ to improve cost structure
FX impact
•
Nearly all revenue is in USD, while ~75% of COGS is sold in NTD
•
Sensitivity of revenue to the USD/TWD exchange rate is ~100%
•
1% appreciation in NTD vs. USD will reduce reported NTD revenue by 1% and GM
by 0.4ppt

•
N2P - featuring better performance and power (MP in 2H26)
•
A16 - with best-in-class superpower rail, SPR, providing 8-10% speed improvement
at same power, 15-20% power improvement at same speed, 7-10% chip density
increase vs. N2P, suitable for specific HPC and dense power delivery network (MP
in 2H26)
•
N2, N2P, A16 will be large and long-lasting nodes for TSMC
A14

Will be in 2 nd  gen nano-sheet transistor structure
•
A14 - 10-15% speed improvement at same power, 20-30% power improvement at

•
Device performance and yield improvements are on or ahead of schedule
•
SPR is planned for 2029

supply demand might be balanced by 2026. Is this still our view? Or do you think
the capacity starts to look tighter?

AI continues to be strong, so does CoWoS
•
We are in a mode of narrowing the gap. The momentum is still there and very
healthy.
On-device AI – are you seeing more development? Is it better than 3-6 months
back?
•
It takes 1-2 years to complete a new design on a product. The momentum is still
going.
•
The edge AI number is mild, and the die size will increase by 5-10% . Need to wait
for around 6 months to 1 year to see an explosion
4Q25 revenue looks like it will decline. Is that based on your customers? Or is it
TSMC being cautious in terms of the guidance?

•

conservative.
•
CC guaranteed that with technology leadership and excellent execution, it will grab
opportunities and achieve the high end of the target

similar level as this year?

FX impact is huge. TSMC is working on selling our value. We are confident about
53% GM and higher - pay more attention to higher
H20 – H20 seems to be shipped to China, can our long term AI accelerator growth
of mid 40% CAGR be higher?
•
TSMC didn’t see the signal. It is too early to give an estimate now.
•
This is really positive for TSMC and its customers
•
TSMC is not ready to increase its forecast, so it's probably more appropriate to
answer this in another quarter.
N2 ramp – What will be the revenue contribution next year? It’s surprising that N2
ramp is similar to N3. Can we expect 15% revenue contribution from N2 in 2026
and 10-11% in 2027?
•
TSMC ramps up new node with smartphone being the first application. Now, it’s not
only smartphones but HPC products.
•
Ramping profile is similar to N3 due to limitation of our capacity
•
Revenue contribution will be bigger – N2 should not have the same price as N3
N5/N3 – the supply and demand for N5/N3. N5 conversion seems to be down, as
well as N3/N5 conversion. But we don’t see capacity expansion on N3. Does that
mean N5 will be less utilized? Or should we try to build more N3 in the future?
•
N3 capacity is very tight. It will continue for a couple of years
•
N5 is also very tight – because some AI products still use N4, and will transition to
N3 in the next 2 years
•
TSMC’s advantage is that it has a giga Fab cluster. We have 85-90% common tools
for each node
•
It uses N7 to support N5, converting N5 to N3. Our leading edge capacities are all
very tight
GM – To what extent can TSMC adjust wafer pricing higher to neutralize cost
increases in your business?
•
When FX is against TSMC, it can lean on other factors (the 6 factors for the
profitability) to mitigate the negative impact
•
Raising the price is only one of the factors that it can leverage
•
It believes GM 53% and higher is still achievable
AI in factories – How much economic benefit can TSMC get from applying AI to
the fabs? Any gains on the cost structure?
•
It uses AI in operations, manufacturing and R&D
•
1% productivity gains in a company of its size equals to US$1bn gains
11 fabs in Taiwan – do we have enough capacity to support the strong demand to
next year, and also to N2, and will we further convert more N5 to N3? How do you
see the N2 capacity plan for 2026?
•
TSMC saw lots of announcements on AI datacenters around the world, and demand
for N2, N3, and N5 is very high
15

18 July 2025
gokul.hariharan@jpmorgan.com
•
It tries very hard to narrow the gap of demand and supply
N2 – What is the ROI of N2 vs. N3? The capex is higher, and the company yield on
N2 is also pretty good, what is the development for N2?
•
N2 profitability is better than N3
•
N3 – it takes longer to catch up with the company average
•
N2 – it should be back to the past level
•
In the past, the corporate average GM was 50% and now it is 53%. So it’s less
meaningful to talk about how much time it takes to catch up with the corporate
average
•
N2 development is on track, ramping in 2H25. Revenue will come up in 1H26
Capex – 2025 guidance is stronger on AI demand, but we stay more conservative
on the capex? Is it because of macro uncertainty or any constraint in construction?
What is the capex outlook for 2026/27?
•
Capex is based on the following year’s business
•
TSMC is mindful of all macro uncertainties when considering capex plans
•
It is too early to talk about 2026, but it’s unlikely to see sudden drop in capex dollar
amounts in the following years
Cloud AI growth – What is the AI accelerator revenue growth we expect in 2025?
What is our CoWoS capacity expansion plan for 2025? What is the plan for
CoWoS capacity in 2026?
•
It tries to narrow the gap for now and 2026
•
Demand is strong and healthy, and it's building new facilities in the back-end to
increase CoWoS capacity
•
AI demand is really strong, so is CoWoS capacity
Advanced packaging – The die size is getting bigger, requiring more power
consumption and energy efficiency. What is our strategy for advanced packaging
along with advanced node development? Any solutions we are prioritizing? What
about the timeline and road map?
•
Timeline is based on customers. It develops technology and increases capacity when
the customer has such demand
•
For advanced packaging, customers have different approaches. So we develop
different technologies for all the customers, which is related to leading edge
technology.
•
There are some similarities in the various technologies, or it will take too much
effort and get no return
Mature node – There is overcapacity industry-wide for the older node. Can we
consolidate different nodes and how do we protect our profitability?
•
TSMC develops specialty for older node (e.g. RF technology, CMOS, or high
voltage)
•
It is not worried about overcapacity, otherwise it will not build fabs in Germany and
Japan. It’s all related to customer demand
16

18 July 2025
gokul.hariharan@jpmorgan.com
Humanoid robot – We start to see some contributions from robots, how does
TSMC evaluate the market size? What are the opportunities in the long run for
leading edge and mature node?
•
It’s too early to talk about it in 2025. Humanoid is too complicated, it will be used in
the medical industry most of the time
•
A lot of sensor tech. It is complex because it deals with human directly
•
Its customer think EV cars are nothing, as robots will be 10 times of EV
Pricing – Do we see customers pulling in earlier than in 2026? More color on
4Q25?
•
No. TSMC hasn’t seen any different customer behavior so far.
•
N3 cycle time is 4 months - there’s no way to pull in anything, and the capacity is
really tight. We have all the schedules and little room for pulling
Capital intensity – When investing in a new node, we see capital intensity jumping
to >40%. We see strong demand for N2 for multiple years, what is your expectation
on capital intensity?
•
Capex is invested in the future growth opportunities
•
If TSMC does its job well, we should see higher growth in revenue than the growth
in capex, where there shouldn’t be high capital intensity
AI adoption of leading edge node – how do we see the AI adoption of the most
leading edge node for TSMC? How do we see that going forward with A16?
•
HPC customers are usually one step behind, usually N+1 or N+2
•
Power consumption is very important. Data center suppliers build electricity plants
to support their AI data centers
Overseas expansion – TSMC is speeding up its US 2nd fab, noting the US ITC bill.
How does this impact our US expansion and any implication on overseas dilution?
•
The ramp-up schedule is based on customer demand. It appreciates the US
government increasing the ITC from 25% to 35%
•
Margin impact should be positive but not significant in the 5 year period
US investment – Does speeding up US investment impact other regional
developments in Japan and Germany? What is the breakdown of overseas vs.
domestic capex going forward?
•
US Fab: for the leading-edge
•
Japan Fab: for specialty nodes, specifically for CMOS sensors
•
Germany Fab: for the automotive industry
•
They are not in the same field, so it should not affect fab investment in Japan and
Germany
17

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC  (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly
position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and
N2) and industry-leading packaging technology. We believe TSMC could grow low-mid
30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pick-
up (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026. Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3
yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the
positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the
impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in
2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

body_anchor_checks.text: The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution. We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures. Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026. While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared. As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures. Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026. While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared. As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%). We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand. We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275. In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes. Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

body_anchor_checks.text: • Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25. Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check. But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence. We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues). But 4Q25 should be the near- term bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026. We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

body_anchor_checks.text: • Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view. We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029). Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies. We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

body_anchor_checks.text: now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm. Hence, 5-6% wafer shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term. For 2026, we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices. We believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of CoWoS. Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.

body_anchor_checks.text: • N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.

body_anchor_checks.text: We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.

body_anchor_checks.text: • Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q. We believe that TSMC is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point. TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view). We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared. Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for many years. We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24. Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.

body_anchor_checks.text: • Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
body_anchor_checks.source_at_anchors: • Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand. We expect 2026 capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026). We also expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing. We believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

TSMC
Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.
• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).
But 4Q25 should be the nearterm bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026.
We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.
• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies.
We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
Hence, 5-6% wafer shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term.
For 2026, we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices.
We believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of CoWoS.
Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
• Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
We believe that TSMC is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point.
TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for many years.
We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
We expect 2026 capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
We also expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
We believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better
TSMC reported a stronger-than-expected 2Q GM of 58.6%, beating both JPMe and Consensus by 0.7-1ppt and reaching the high-end of its guidance (57-59%) despite unfavorable FX (around 125bps impact) thanks to higher-than-expected UTR and cost improvement efforts.
Company guided 3Q rev to grow 8% qoq at mid point, with GM likely at 55.5-57.5% (down 2.1ppts qoq at mid point).
The margin guidance is quite impressive in our view, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
While 4Q GM would likely further decline with the UTR draw down, we expect 4Q25 to be the near-term bottom for GMs.
2H25 should be the period with maximum stress on GMs (fastest period of TWD appreciation so far in 3Q25, overseas cost dilution, some negate demand impact dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).
Even in this period, TSMC appears to be able to hold GMs well above 53%, demonstrating its underlying pricing power and operational efficiency.
Without the recent TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this point.
With price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026, we expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

Pricing uptick coming through; Double-digit blended ASP
increases now the norm
TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases, including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25.
Given strong pricing power and intention to raise pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward.
As a result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth, which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over the long term.
With TSMC indicating that capacity remains tight, particularly for N5 and N3, and a faster ramp-up of N2, we anticipate pricing to rise in 2026 (6-10% increase in leadingedge wafer prices, along with higher pricing for overseas fabs) to offset cost increases, some impact of TWD appreciation and overseas expansion.

N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and
HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel
We’ve mentioned in our previous notes (link, link) that N2 progress appears to be quite strong.
In the first 15 months of N2 ramp, we see AMD (ramping in late 2025), Apple, Mediatek, Qualcomm and Intel (likely ramping in 2026) all starting their N2 wafers at TSMC.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and Mediatek should also adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains as an upside risk.
While the capacity agreement with TSMC for N2 has not yet signed, this looks increasingly likely given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products (starting likely from Novalake) are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe, due to competitive reasons (AMD and Apple Macs moving to N2 in 2027).
We continue to expect TSMC to build 20k wfpm / 60-65k wfpm by end 2025/2026.
N2 wafer pricing is likely to come in at ~20-25% higher than N3E, with $26-27k pricing for mobile versions of N2, while HPC versions with higher metal layer count are likely to be more expensive.
A faster ramp for N2, compared to N3, is expected, and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (versus $3.5bn of first year revenues for N3).

Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness
in 4Q
In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s.
While we’ve already highlighted the potential guidance raise (link), the magnitude turns out to be slightly above our expectation of high-20s.
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around 10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of 1%/6% qoq decline.
We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in 3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
While we do believe that there has been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40% yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

Capex outlook and Dividend growth
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy) in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
While the Capex seems to be high in terms of dollar amount, management also emphasized that sales growth would outgrow the capex growth.
We anticipate capital intensity likely to be down to ~30% in 2027 versus 40-50% in 2023-25.
Meanwhile, we believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

sentences.text: Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).
But 4Q25 should be the nearterm bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026.
We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).

Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies.
We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better

TSMC reported a stronger-than-expected 2Q GM of 58.6%, beating both JPMe and Consensus by 0.7-1ppt and reaching the high-end of its guidance (57-59%) despite unfavorable FX (around 125bps impact) thanks to higher-than-expected UTR and cost improvement efforts.
Company guided 3Q rev to grow 8% qoq at mid point, with GM likely at 55.5-57.5% (down 2.1ppts qoq at mid point).
The margin guidance is quite impressive in our view, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
While 4Q GM would likely further decline with the UTR draw down, we expect 4Q25 to be the near-term bottom for GMs.

2H25 should be the period with maximum stress on GMs (fastest period of TWD appreciation so far in 3Q25, overseas cost dilution, some negate demand impact dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).
Even in this period, TSMC appears to be able to hold GMs well above 53%, demonstrating its underlying pricing power and operational efficiency.
Without the recent TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this point.
With price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026, we expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

Risks to Rating and Price Target

Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.
