Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.

emand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.

• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.

s robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target

TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

TSMC
Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.
• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).
But 4Q25 should be the nearterm bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026.
We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.
• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies.
We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
Hence, 5-6% wafer shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term.
For 2026, we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices.
We believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of CoWoS.
Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
• Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
We believe that TSMC is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point.
TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for many years.
We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
We expect 2026 capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
We also expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
We believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better
TSMC reported a stronger-than-expected 2Q GM of 58.6%, beating both JPMe and Consensus by 0.7-1ppt and reaching the high-end of its guidance (57-59%) despite unfavorable FX (around 125bps impact) thanks to higher-than-expected UTR and cost improvement efforts.
Company guided 3Q rev to grow 8% qoq at mid point, with GM likely at 55.5-57.5% (down 2.1ppts qoq at mid point).
The margin guidance is quite impressive in our view, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
While 4Q GM would likely further decline with the UTR draw down, we expect 4Q25 to be the near-term bottom for GMs.
2H25 should be the period with maximum stress on GMs (fastest period of TWD appreciation so far in 3Q25, overseas cost dilution, some negate demand impact dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).
Even in this period, TSMC appears to be able to hold GMs well above 53%, demonstrating its underlying pricing power and operational efficiency.
Without the recent TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this point.
With price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026, we expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases, including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25.

In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s.

Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around 10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of 1%/6% qoq decline.
We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in 3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

TSMC
Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.
• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).
But 4Q25 should be the nearterm bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026.
We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.
• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies.
We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
Hence, 5-6% wafer shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term.
For 2026, we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices.
We believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of CoWoS.
Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
• Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
We believe that TSMC is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point.
TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for many years.
We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
We expect 2026 capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
We also expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
We believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

Without the recent TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this point.

TSMC has now seen more than 10 quarters of double-digit YoY ASP increases, including a 16% YoY rise in 2Q25.
Given strong pricing power and intention to raise pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward.
As a result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth, which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over the long term.
With TSMC indicating that capacity remains tight, particularly for N5 and N3, and a faster ramp-up of N2, we anticipate pricing to rise in 2026 (6-10% increase in leadingedge wafer prices, along with higher pricing for overseas fabs) to offset cost increases, some impact of TWD appreciation and overseas expansion.

N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and
HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel
We’ve mentioned in our previous notes (link, link) that N2 progress appears to be quite strong.
In the first 15 months of N2 ramp, we see AMD (ramping in late 2025), Apple, Mediatek, Qualcomm and Intel (likely ramping in 2026) all starting their N2 wafers at TSMC.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and Mediatek should also adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains as an upside risk.
While the capacity agreement with TSMC for N2 has not yet signed, this looks increasingly likely given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products (starting likely from Novalake) are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe, due to competitive reasons (AMD and Apple Macs moving to N2 in 2027).
We continue to expect TSMC to build 20k wfpm / 60-65k wfpm by end 2025/2026.
N2 wafer pricing is likely to come in at ~20-25% higher than N3E, with $26-27k pricing for mobile versions of N2, while HPC versions with higher metal layer count are likely to be more expensive.
A faster ramp for N2, compared to N3, is expected, and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (versus $3.5bn of first year revenues for N3).

Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness
in 4Q
In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s.
While we’ve already highlighted the potential guidance raise (link), the magnitude turns out to be slightly above our expectation of high-20s.
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around 10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of 1%/6% qoq decline.
We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in 3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
While we do believe that there has been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40% yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

Capex outlook and Dividend growth
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy) in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
While the Capex seems to be high in terms of dollar amount, management also emphasized that sales growth would outgrow the capex growth.
We anticipate capital intensity likely to be down to ~30% in 2027 versus 40-50% in 2023-25.
Meanwhile, we believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.

Investment Thesis, Valuation and Risks
TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

TSMC
Margin test passed; On to 2026 with strong AI and N2 growth, with upside to GMs from pricing
The strongest message from TSMC’s 2Q25 earnings conference was the resilience of GMs, despite unprecedentedly steep TWD appreciation and increased overseas Fab dilution.
We expect 4Q25 to be the GM trough (due to UTR draw-down), with GMs likely to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Demand trends for AI are strong with broader demand pickup (CSPs, sovereign AI and China demand) and CoWoS capacity likely to remain tight into 2026.
While TSMC is cautious on 4Q25 (we now model 6% qoq decline in revenues), chances are that demand could shape up better if tariffs turn out to be less intense than feared.
As such, we believe TSMC could eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).
We continue to see healthy growth in 2026, with a faster N2 ramp, price hikes from1Q26 and continued strength in N3 due to strong AI accelerator demand.
We raise our FY25/ FY26 EPS estimates by 5/4% to reflect stronger growth prospects in AI and stay OW with a Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275.
In the near term, we believe the stock may stay rangebound as the market is likely to focus on Sec 232 and specific country tariff outcomes.
Once some clarity emerges on this front, we believe the stock should start pricing in strong growth and GM rebound in 2026, with some prospect of meaningful N2 outsourcing from Intel.
• Passing the GM test; 2026 should look better: TSMC’s 3Q Gross Margin guidance (55.5-57.5%, JPMe 56.7%) is quite impressive, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD appreciation and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
Increased utilization has helped, but strong cost-cutting measures have also contributed to keeping costs under check.
But for the steep TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC could have easily reached 60+% GM levels by now, demonstrating underlying pricing power and operational excellence.
We believe that 4Q25 GMs are likely to also be down qoq, dragged down by lower utilization (due to the qoq decline in revenues).
But 4Q25 should be the nearterm bottom for GMs, with price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026.
We expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.
• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from China, after H20 resumption, in our view.
We expect Datacenter AI growth expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029).
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution from HBM base-dies.
We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

now the norm: As highlighted before, we believe that TSMC is now in a new period of growth, where double-digit blended ASP growth is the norm.
Hence, 5-6% wafer shipment growth should help drive ~20% growth in revenues, which should also drive capital intensity lower and help drive strong 30+% ROEs over the long-term.
For 2026, we continue to expect leading edge wafer prices to move up again as TSMC reflects increased costs, TWD appreciation, increased overseas mix, etc into the wafer prices.
We believe N3 is likely to see the most upside, followed by N2, N4 and certain forms of CoWoS.
Overall, we see 6-10% price increases across the leading edge process nodes.
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year revenues for N3).
Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research.
Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains the primary upside risk - we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.
• Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness in 4Q: Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness in 4Q.
We believe that TSMC is taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and is not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan at this point.
TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
We are still modeling a 6% qoq decline in 4Q25, but feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
Consumer demand (esp for smartphones and PCs) has also been less price sensitive in recent years, given that these markets have already been ex-growth for many years.
We do believe that there has been some pull-in demand in consumer, PC etc. in 1H25, but the extent is likely to be small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
Overall, we believe that TSMC’s 4Q25 revenues could come in better than guidance, with FY25 ending up with low 30% USD growth.
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand.
We expect 2026 capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
We also expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
We believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

TSMC reported a stronger-than-expected 2Q GM of 58.6%, beating both JPMe and Consensus by 0.7-1ppt and reaching the high-end of its guidance (57-59%) despite unfavorable FX (around 125bps impact) thanks to higher-than-expected UTR and cost improvement efforts.
Company guided 3Q rev to grow 8% qoq at mid point, with GM likely at 55.5-57.5% (down 2.1ppts qoq at mid point).
The margin guidance is quite impressive in our view, considering a 600 bps drag from TWD and 100-200bps from overseas expansion since 1Q25.
While 4Q GM would likely further decline with the UTR draw down, we expect 4Q25 to be the near-term bottom for GMs.
2H25 should be the period with maximum stress on GMs (fastest period of TWD appreciation so far in 3Q25, overseas cost dilution, some negate demand impact dragging utilization lower in 4Q25 with price hikes not kicking in yet).
Even in this period, TSMC appears to be able to hold GMs well above 53%, demonstrating its underlying pricing power and operational efficiency.
Without the recent TWD appreciation, we believe TSMC would have been able to achieve 60+% GMs at this point.
With price hikes and a better N3 mix kicking in from early 2026, we expect GMs to remain higher than 2H25 levels through 2026, despite some dilution in late 2026 as N2 starts ramping up.

Given strong pricing power and intention to raise pricing to reflect increasing costs and technology leadership, we believe that low-mid teens blended ASP growth will become the norm for TSMC moving forward.
As a result, a 5-6% increase in wafer shipments should contribute to ~20% revenue growth, which in turn should likely reduce capital intensity and support strong 30+% ROE over the long term.
With TSMC indicating that capacity remains tight, particularly for N5 and N3, and a faster ramp-up of N2, we anticipate pricing to rise in 2026 (6-10% increase in leadingedge wafer prices, along with higher pricing for overseas fabs) to offset cost increases, some impact of TWD appreciation and overseas expansion.

We’ve mentioned in our previous notes (link, link) that N2 progress appears to be quite strong.

Apple appears increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship SoCs from QCOM and Mediatek should also adopt N2.
We also see small wafer demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products.
Looking into 2027, we believe all leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5.
Intel remains as an upside risk.
While the capacity agreement with TSMC for N2 has not yet signed, this looks increasingly likely given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k wfpm, well below normal peak for a leading edge node).
We anticipate that Intel's client PC products (starting likely from Novalake) are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe, due to competitive reasons (AMD and Apple Macs moving to N2 in 2027).
We continue to expect TSMC to build 20k wfpm / 60-65k wfpm by end 2025/2026.
N2 wafer pricing is likely to come in at ~20-25% higher than N3E, with $26-27k pricing for mobile versions of N2, while HPC versions with higher metal layer count are likely to be more expensive.
A faster ramp for N2, compared to N3, is expected, and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (versus $3.5bn of first year revenues for N3).

Near-term eyes largely on tariffs and the degree of weakness
in 4Q
In the earnings call, TSMC raised 2025 full year guidance to 30% yoy revenue growth in USD terms, from previous guidance of mid- 20s.
While we’ve already highlighted the potential guidance raise (link), the magnitude turns out to be slightly above our expectation of high-20s.
Investor attention is likely to be largely focused on the implied qoq weakness (around 10% qoq revenue decline) in 4Q, which is weaker than Consensus and previous JPMe of 1%/6% qoq decline.
We believe the implied weakness is mainly due to 1) high base in 3Q (rev guidance above market expectations), 2) TSMC taking a conservative view on tariffs (Sec 232 and country-specific tariffs) and not factoring in any exemptions for TSMC or Taiwan-made products at this point, and 3) TSMC also appears to be anticipating a marked slowdown in consumer demand as a result (including iPhone, in our view).
However, we feel that such a sharp slowdown in demand may not materialize, given that tariff outcomes so far have been better than feared.
While we do believe that there has been some pull-in demand, especially in consumer electronics, in 1H25 (1H rev up 40% yoy in USD terms), but the extent is likely small given the ongoing tightness in N5 and N3 capacity since 2H24.
We therefore maintain our 6% qoq decline expectation for 4Q, and expect TSMC to eventually finish the year with low-mid 30% yoy growth in USD terms (JPMe 32%).

Capex outlook and Dividend growth
TSMC maintained its 2025 Capex guidance unchanged at US$38-42bn (up ~30% yoy).
While there’s no further guidance for coming years yet, management only indicated no significant drop in Capex expected, despite very strong N2 demand, which is a bit more guarded, compared to investors’ expectation of capex increase in 2026.
However, we still anticipate continued Capex growth to US$45bn (up 13% yoy) in 2026, and maintained at a high level in 2027 (JPMe~US$40bn) driven by 1) strong N2 demand, 2) continued strength in N3, and 3) continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026).
In addition, we expect N2 demand to be upsized in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing.
While the Capex seems to be high in terms of dollar amount, management also emphasized that sales growth would outgrow the capex growth.
We anticipate capital intensity likely to be down to ~30% in 2027 versus 40-50% in 2023-25.
Meanwhile, we believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.

TSMC (Overweight; Price Target: NT$1275.0)
Investment Thesis
We expect TSMC's structural growth drivers to remain strong due to its near-monopoly position in AI accelerators and edge AI, supported by its robust process roadmap (N3 and N2) and industry-leading packaging technology.
We believe TSMC could grow low-mid 30% in USD terms in 2025 and healthy growth in 2026, driven by broader AI demand pickup (e.g. CSPs, sovereigns and China demand) with CoWoS capacity remaining tight into
2026.
Additionally, we anticipate the GM to rebound in 2026 with price hikes, better N3 yield, and accelerated productivity and cost-down measures.
Valuation
Our Dec-25 PT of NT$1,275 is based on ~20x 12-month forward P/E and reflects the positive fundamental demand driver, continued growth in N3 and stronger N2 ramp in 2026.
Our target multiple is higher than TSMC’s five-year average historical multiple.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Key downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) uncertainty regarding the impact of tariffs and a global economic slowdown; (2) worse-than-expected AI demand in 2026; and (3) greater GM dilution from US fabs due to the faster ramp.

• Datacenter AI growth looks stronger; continued growth in 2026 with N3 
migration kicking in: TSMC indicated that Datacenter AI demand growth 
appears stronger with strong token growth at hyperscalers, upside from 
sovereign AI demand and likely upside materializing in a few months from 
China, after H20 resumption, in our view. We expect Datacenter AI growth 
expectations to be revised up again (from current mid 40% CAGR into 2029). 
Looking into 2026, we expect 50-60% growth in Datacenter AI, helped by 
strong growth in CoWoS capacity for AI accelerators, better pricing due to 
migration of most accelerators from N4 to N3 and incremental contribution 
from HBM base-dies. We believe that CoWoS demand expectations are likely 
to be raised again (after a couple of rounds of cuts in 1H25), especially if NVDA 
starts orders H20 and B20 related products for the China market.

source_records.raw_text:
• N2 ramp appears faster and smoother; Broad smartphone and HPC adoption, with 
upside risk from Intel: We expect N2 to ramp to be 60-65k wfpm of output by end 2026, 
a faster ramp than N3 and should contribute $6.8bn of revenues in 2026 (~2x of first year 
revenues for N3). Yield ramp for N2 also appears quite smooth with initial chip probing 
yield already reaching 70% for early products, based on our research. Apple appears 
increasingly likely to use N2 for all four new iPhones in 2H26, while Android flagship 
SoCs from QCOM and MediaTek are also likely to adopt N2. We also see small wafer 
demand for AMD and Intel for their N2 products. Looking into 2027, we believe all 
leading edge customers except NVDA are likely to be shipping N2 based products - a 
much faster adoption curve compared to N3 or N5. Intel remains the primary upside risk 
- we believe that Intel is yet to sign a capacity agreement with TSMC for N2, but this looks 
increasingly likely, given the scale down of Intel 18A (likely only 1 phase of 25-30k 
wfpm, well below the normal peak for a leading edge node). We anticipate that Intel's 
client PC products are likely to be outsourced to TSMC N2 in 2027-28 timeframe.

source_records.raw_text:
• Capex outlook mixed, but we expect upside in 2026; Strong, multiyear dividend 
growth ahead: TSMC’s commentary on capex was more mixed, and did not indicate 
continued growth in capex into 2026, despite very strong N2 demand. We expect 2026 
capex to grow to $45bn, driven by strong N2 demand, continued strength in N3 and 
continued accelerated buildout of capacity in the US (tools move in for the 2nd AZ Fab 
and construction of 3rd and 4th AZ Fab in 2026). We also expect N2 demand to be upsized 
in case Intel signs a capacity agreement with TSMC for large-scale N2 outsourcing. We 
believe that TSMC’s cash dividends should grow steadily due to strong FCF generation, 
and expect a 2023-27 DPS CAGR of 26%, with 2027E dividends reaching NT$33 levels.
